conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/religionRol: Lebanon’s political system allocated power by religious community, and its militias were overwhelmingly confessional — Maronite Christian, Sunni, Shi‘a and Druze — so the war is often described as Christian against Muslim. Most historians, however, including Theodor Hanf, Kamal Salibi and Fawwaz Traboulsi, stress that confession functioned as political community rather than theology: the conflict concerned the distribution of power, the armed Palestinian presence, class inequality and the interventions of Syria, Israel, Iran and others. Alliances crossed religious lines — Christians fought Christians in 1978 and 1988–90, and Shi‘a Amal fought Palestinians and Hezbollah — and some Christian clergy and Maronite monastic orders openly supported the Christian militias, while others worked for reconciliation. Religion was a contributing marker and mobiliser rather than the cause.

conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/summary: From 1975 to 1990 Lebanon’s confessional political system collapsed into a war of militias divided largely by religious community, entangled with the Palestinian, Syrian, Israeli and Iranian struggles in the region. Massacres were committed by all sides — Karantina, Damour, Tel al-Zaatar, Sabra and Shatila, the Chouf. The Taif Agreement of 1989 ended the war by reapportioning power between Christians and Muslims, leaving Syria dominant until 2005.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/story:
Modern Lebanon was built on a balance between religious communities. Mount Lebanon’s Maronite Christians had enjoyed autonomy under the Ottomans after the Druze–Christian massacres of 1860, and the French mandate created Greater Lebanon in 1920 with a slim Christian majority. The unwritten National Pact of 1943 gave the presidency to a Maronite, the premiership to a Sunni and the speakership to a Shi‘a, and fixed parliamentary seats at six Christians to five Muslims, based on the census of 1932, the last ever held. By the 1970s Muslims, especially the poorer Shi‘a of the south and the Beirut suburbs, were a majority, and they and the left demanded reform that the Maronite establishment resisted.

The Palestinian presence upset the balance. Refugees from 1948 lived in camps, and after the PLO was expelled from Jordan in 1970–71 its fighters made Lebanon their base; the 1969 Cairo Agreement gave them autonomy in the camps. Many Christians saw an armed ‘state within the state’, while the Sunni, Druze and leftist Lebanese National Movement under Kamal Jumblatt saw the Palestinians as allies. Israeli reprisals against PLO raids fell on southern Lebanon. Both sides armed militias in the early 1970s.

On 13 April 1975 gunmen fired on the Phalangist leader Pierre Gemayel outside a church in Ain el-Remmaneh, killing several people; hours later Phalangists ambushed a bus carrying Palestinians, killing about two dozen. Fighting spread through Beirut, divided along the ‘Green Line’ into a Christian east and a Muslim west. Killings at checkpoints on the basis of religion recorded on identity cards became common — on ‘Black Saturday’, 6 December 1975, Phalangists killed scores of Muslims. In January 1976 Christian militias overran the Karantina slum, killing hundreds, and Palestinian and leftist forces sacked the Christian town of Damour, killing hundreds of civilians. In August 1976 the Christian militias took the Tel al-Zaatar refugee camp after a long siege, followed by massacres. Syria intervened in June 1976 — at first on the Christian side — and its Arab Deterrent Force stayed. Kamal Jumblatt was assassinated in March 1977, after which Druze killed many Christian villagers in the Chouf.

The war fractured further. In 1978 Bashir Gemayel’s forces killed his rival Tony Frangieh and his family at Ehden, and turned against the Syrians; Israel invaded the south in 1978 and set up a proxy militia. The Shi‘a cleric Musa al-Sadr, founder of Amal, vanished in Libya in 1978, and after the Iranian revolution Shi‘a militancy grew. In June 1982 Israel invaded to destroy the PLO, besieged West Beirut and secured the PLO’s evacuation by sea. Bashir Gemayel was elected president but was assassinated on 14 September 1982; between 16 and 18 September Lebanese Forces militiamen, in areas controlled by the Israeli army, massacred hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila camps. The Israeli Kahan Commission found Defence Minister Ariel Sharon indirectly responsible.

After Israel withdrew from the Chouf in 1983 the ‘Mountain War’ between the Druze and the Lebanese Forces led to massacres and the flight of tens of thousands of Christians from villages where they had lived beside Druze for centuries. Suicide bombings destroyed the US embassy and, on 23 October 1983, the US Marine and French barracks, killing 241 Americans and 58 French soldiers; the new Iranian-backed Hezbollah emerged and seized Western hostages. Amal fought the Palestinians in the ‘War of the Camps’ (1985–88) and then Hezbollah. In 1988 parliament failed to elect a president, and Michel Aoun, the army commander, headed a rival military government; his 1989 ‘war of liberation’ against Syria and his 1990 ‘war of elimination’ against Samir Geagea’s Lebanese Forces devastated the Christian heartland.

In October 1989 Lebanese deputies meeting at Taif in Saudi Arabia agreed to a new settlement: equal Christian and Muslim representation in parliament, a transfer of executive power from the Maronite president to the Sunni-led cabinet, the disarming of militias and recognition of Syria’s special role. The Maronite Patriarch Nasrallah Boutros Sfeir backed the accord against Aoun’s opposition. On 13 October 1990 Syrian forces attacked the presidential palace at Baabda and Aoun fled to the French embassy. An amnesty law of 1991 pardoned most wartime crimes; the militias, except Hezbollah, disarmed.

The war left perhaps 120,000–150,000 dead, around 17,000 missing and up to a million people displaced. Christian emigration accelerated, reducing their share of the population. Syria occupied Lebanon until 2005, Israel the south until 2000, and the confessional system, confirmed rather than abolished, continues to shape Lebanese politics. Pope John Paul II called Lebanon ‘more than a country: it is a message of freedom and an example of pluralism’ in 1989, convened a Special Synod for Lebanon in 1995 and visited in 1997.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/nameOfGod: Christian militias wore crosses and images of saints and the Virgin, and some presented their cause as the survival of the last free Christian homeland in the Middle East; the Lebanese Maronite Order of monks, under its superior Fr Charbel Kassis, gave money, land and fighters to the Lebanese Front, and the Kaslik monks’ university supported its ideology. On the Muslim side, Islamist movements, especially Hezbollah from 1982, framed the struggle against Israel and the West as jihad. Leaders on all sides, however, usually spoke the language of nation, community and survival rather than of holy war.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/religiousCa: The confessional political system of the 1943 National Pact tied power to religious community and froze it on the 1932 census.
Maronite fears of becoming a minority in a Muslim Arab world and of losing Lebanon’s character as a Christian refuge.
Muslim, especially Shi‘a, grievances at under-representation and deprivation in a system dominated by Christians and Sunni notables.
Memories of nineteenth-century Druze–Maronite massacres and communal fears of extermination.
The rise of political Islam after 1979, with Iran sponsoring Hezbollah.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/otherCauses: The armed PLO presence after 1970 and Israeli reprisals turned Lebanon into a front of the Arab–Israeli conflict.
Severe social inequality between Beirut’s prosperous elites and the rural poor and slum dwellers.
A weak state and army, unable to control rival militias or the Palestinian organisations.
Intervention by Syria, Israel, Iran, Iraq, Libya and the Cold War superpowers, each backing local clients.
Rivalries between leading families and warlords within each community.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/triggers/0: The attack on Pierre Gemayel at Ain el-Remmaneh and the Phalangist ambush of a Palestinian bus on 13 April 1975.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/triggers/1: The breakdown of the army along confessional lines in early 1976.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/triggers/2: The Syrian intervention of June 1976 and the Israeli invasions of 1978 and 1982.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/0/: The National Pact allocates power among religious communities at independence.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/1/: The Cairo Agreement recognises PLO autonomy in Lebanon’s refugee camps.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/2/: Ain el-Remmaneh bus massacre (13 April) begins the war; Black Saturday killings in Beirut (6 December).
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/3/: Karantina and Damour massacres (January); Syrian intervention (June); fall of Tel al-Zaatar (August).
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/4/: Kamal Jumblatt assassinated; reprisal killings of Christians in the Chouf.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/5/: Israel’s Litani operation; Ehden massacre; Musa al-Sadr disappears in Libya.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/6/: Israeli invasion and siege of West Beirut; PLO evacuation; Bashir Gemayel assassinated; Sabra and Shatila massacre (16–18 September).
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/7/: Mountain War in the Chouf; bombings of the US embassy and the Multinational Force barracks.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/8/: Hezbollah publishes its Open Letter; War of the Camps begins.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/9/: Aoun’s war against Syria; John Paul II’s letter on Lebanon as a ‘message’; Taif Agreement (October).
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/10: Intra-Christian war between Aoun and the Lebanese Forces; Syrian assault ends Aoun’s government (13 October).
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/11: General amnesty law; militias other than Hezbollah disarm.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/timeline/12: John Paul II visits Lebanon after the Special Synod for Lebanon.

conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/casualties/: Estimates of deaths from 1975 to 1990 usually range from about 120,000 to 150,000; a frequently cited count by Labaki and Abou Rjeily gives around 144,000. Some 17,000 people remain missing, and up to a million were displaced at some point. Because no census or official death registry was kept, all figures are approximate.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effects/0: The Taif Agreement of 1989 equalised Christian and Muslim parliamentary representation and shifted executive power to the Sunni prime minister and cabinet.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effects/1: Syria dominated Lebanon until 2005 and Israel occupied the south until 2000.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effects/2: Hezbollah emerged as the only armed militia to keep its weapons, becoming a dominant political and military force.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effects/3: Mass emigration, especially of Christians, and the destruction of central Beirut transformed the country.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effects/4: The 1991 amnesty and the absence of a truth process left wartime crimes and the missing unaddressed.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/effectsOnCh: Christian communities lost population and political primacy, with whole regions such as the Chouf emptied of Christians for years.
The involvement of some Maronite clergy and monks with militias provoked criticism within and beyond the Church.
The Maronite patriarchate under Sfeir became a national moral authority by backing Taif and later Lebanese sovereignty.
John Paul II’s Special Synod for Lebanon (1995) and apostolic exhortation A New Hope for Lebanon (1997) urged Christian–Muslim coexistence.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/legacy: The Lebanese war is a cautionary example of how a system designed to give religious communities security can turn them into armed political blocs. It also showed Christians as both perpetrators and victims, and produced voices — Christian and Muslim — who insisted that Lebanon’s plural society was worth preserving.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/dissenters/: The Melkite archbishop of Beirut, known as the ‘red bishop’, called for a secular state and campaigned against confessionalism; he founded the Social Movement and was removed from his see in 1975 by his synod.
The Maronite Patriarch condemned the fratricidal Christian wars of 1988–90 and backed the Taif compromise despite fierce opposition from Aoun’s supporters.
He made repeated appeals for peace, called for a day of prayer for Lebanon and in 1989 described Lebanon as a ‘message’ of coexistence for East and West.
The Greek Orthodox Metropolitan of Mount Lebanon wrote throughout the war against militia violence and for Christian–Muslim dialogue.
conflicts/lebanese-civil-war/campaigns/0: Israel’s 1982 invasion and the siege of Beirut
Israel Defense Forces under Defence Minister Ariel Sharon

Launched on 6 June 1982, the invasion advanced up the coast, overrunning Palestinian camps around Tyre and Sidon, and besieged West Beirut for some ten weeks until the PLO agreed to evacuate in August; in September Israeli forces entered West Beirut, where the Sabra and Shatila massacre followed.
